title: Poland Scrambles Fighter Jets as Russian Strikes Hit Western Ukraine
excerpt: Poland reported no airspace violation after scrambling jets during overnight strikes that cut power to 370,000 people in Volyn, as Bulgaria asked NATO for aircraft and anti-drone systems.
body:
• Poland scrambled fighter jets on Friday as Russian attacks overnight hit western Ukraine close to its border, and reported no violation of its airspace.
  • Strikes on the Volyn region, which borders Poland, cut electricity to 370,000 people and injured two, its governor said.
  • A drone attack in Kharkiv killed three people and injured five, while strikes on an apartment block in Uman injured a similar number.
  • Bulgaria said on Friday it has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to strengthen its defences.

Poland scrambled fighter jets on Friday during Russian attacks overnight on western Ukraine, close to the Polish border. The Polish armed forces said no violation of the country's airspace was recorded.

The heaviest reported impact near the border was in Volyn, the western Ukrainian region adjoining Poland. Its governor, Roman Romaniuk, said strikes cut electricity to 370,000 people and injured two. Private power company DTEK said it had imposed emergency power cuts in Kyiv as the attacks continued.

Attacks Across Ukraine, and a Reply

The overnight strikes were not confined to the west. In Kharkiv, in eastern Ukraine, a drone attack killed three people and injured five, the regional governor said. In central Ukraine, police said a strike on an apartment block in Uman injured a similar number.

Ukraine also struck back. Russian officials said air defences blocked a Ukrainian drone attack on a heating plant in the Vladimir region, and Russia said it shot down 644 Ukrainian drones overnight, 94 of them headed for Moscow. Moscow's four airports and St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport suspended operations, Al Jazeera reported from Moscow, and the Russian-installed governor of the Luhansk region said Ukrainian attacks killed two people there.

"We are awaiting their decision."

— Dimitar Stoyanov, Bulgaria's Defence Minister, on the request to NATO

NATO's Eastern Flank Is Asking for More

Concern along NATO's eastern flank has grown since the summer, as Romania, Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states reported repeated drone intrusions into their airspace and waters. In recent weeks drones have struck at least seven cargo ships off the Black Sea coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, leaving 25 people dead or missing, and a hit on a commercial vessel that sank off Bulgaria's coast this week prompted Sofia to summon Russia's ambassador.

On Friday, Bulgaria's Prime Minister Rumen Radev said the evidence pointed to Russia but his government did not have proof. Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov then told reporters Bulgaria had formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and anti-drone systems. He said letters had gone to the NATO Secretary General and the Supreme Allied Commander, and that he planned to meet his Romanian and Turkish counterparts soon to coordinate a common approach in the Black Sea. Bulgaria also expects to join a NATO anti-drone initiative by the end of October, and Romania's president has said his country has asked for additional equipment. NATO did not immediately respond to a request for comment, Reuters reported.

What Comes Next

Poland's scramble ended without an airspace violation, as previous alerts have. The pattern, however, is now wider than one border: two NATO members on the Black Sea are seeking additional allied aircraft and anti-drone systems, and their request will test how quickly the alliance moves from monitoring intrusions to stationing more hardware on its eastern edge. For Ukraine, the immediate task is restoration in Volyn, where hundreds of thousands of people lost power within sight of the Polish frontier.
